framework_choice.document_used: Hu, N., Pavlou, P.A., Zhang, J., "On Self-Selection Biases in Online Product Reviews," MIS Quarterly, 2017 -- https://misq.umn.edu/misq/article/41/2/449/335/On-Self-Selection-Biases-in-Online-Product
framework_choice.justification: The J-shaped/bimodal distribution framework directly applies here: with 5,750 Trustpilot reviews the sample is non-trivial but structurally over-represents strong reactions, so the three recurring negative themes (pricing, denials, slow claims) are treated as confirmed pain signals for a vocal minority, while the silent moderate-majority base rate is assumed to be better than the raw mix implies.

results.text:
Fred Reichheld's 2003 Harvard Business Review article "The One Number You
Need to Grow" introduced the Net Promoter Score after two years of research
linking survey responses to actual customer behavior (repurchasing,
referrals) and ultimately to company growth. The core finding: across most
industries studied, a single question -- "How likely are you to recommend
this company to a friend or colleague?" (0-10 scale) -- was a stronger
predictor of growth than most longer satisfaction surveys. Customers are
bucketed into promoters (9-10), passives (7-8), and detractors (0-6); NPS =
%promoters - %detractors. The methodological lesson for reading any public
sentiment signal (Trustpilot rating, app-store rating, etc.) even when you
don't have the raw NPS survey: a single aggregate score is a legitimate,
research-backed proxy for word-of-mouth growth risk, but it should be read
alongside the volume and recency of responses, not in isolation -- a
4.1/5 rating from a small or stale sample carries much less signal than the
same score from a large, recent sample, since the original NPS research
depended on having enough responses to be statistically meaningful.
results.source: Fred Reichheld, "The One Number You Need to Grow," Harvard Business Review, Dec 2003 -- https://hbr.org/2003/12/the-one-number-you-need-to-grow

results.text:
Hu, Pavlou, and Zhang's research ("Why Do Online Product Reviews Have a
J-Shaped Distribution?", Communications of the ACM 2009; expanded as "On
Self-Selection Biases in Online Product Reviews," MIS Quarterly 2017)
identifies two structural biases in any public review/complaint dataset.
"Acquisition bias": people who already had a favorable predisposition toward
a product are more likely to have bought it and thus more likely to be among
the reviewers at all. "Underreporting bias": people with extreme experiences
(very good or very bad) are far more likely to write a review than people
with a moderate, unremarkable experience -- producing the characteristic
J-shaped (bimodal, skewed) distribution of online ratings rather than a
normal distribution centered on the "typical" customer experience. The
practical implication for reading Trustpilot-style data or complaint themes:
treat the sample as systematically over-representing strong reactions in
both directions, not as a representative cross-section of all customers --
recurring negative themes are real signal about what upsets the most vocal
minority, but the underlying base rate among silent, moderately-satisfied
customers is almost certainly better than the raw review mix suggests.
results.source: Hu, N., Pavlou, P.A., Zhang, J., "On Self-Selection Biases in Online Product Reviews," MIS Quarterly, 2017 -- https://misq.umn.edu/misq/article/41/2/449/335/On-Self-Selection-Biases-in-Online-Product

results.text:
Braun and Clarke's six-phase thematic analysis method is the standard
academic approach for turning unstructured qualitative feedback (reviews,
complaint text, open-ended survey answers) into reliable named themes
rather than impressionistic summaries. The six phases: (1) familiarize
yourself with the full dataset before coding anything, (2) generate initial
codes -- short labels applied consistently across the data, (3) search for
candidate themes by grouping related codes, (4) review themes against the
full dataset to check they actually hold up and aren't just one or two loud
examples, (5) clearly define and name each theme so it has one core
meaning, not several blended ideas, (6) produce the write-up connecting
each theme back to specific supporting examples. The discipline this
imposes when reading a small set of public complaint themes: a theme is
only as credible as its review (step 4) -- if a "theme" is really just one
vivid complaint generalized into a pattern, it should be labeled as an
isolated anecdote, not presented with the same confidence as a theme that
recurs across many independent reviews. The process is explicitly iterative,
not a one-pass classification -- themes should be revisited as more
evidence comes in.
results.source: Braun, V. & Clarke, V., reflexive thematic analysis six-phase framework (Qualitative Research in Psychology, 2006; subsequent methodology papers) -- https://www.thedegreedoctor.com/blog/braun-and-clarke-thematic-analysis-how-to-do-the-six-step-process-in-your-qualitative-research-project
